tagline: Lumber and salt fortunes built a neighborhood along Center Avenue.
intro: Center Avenue carries M-25 through Bay City’s historic residential neighborhood, where Italianate, Queen Anne and Châteauesque houses stand among later architectural styles. Michigan’s Department of Transportation designated the stretch from Madison Avenue to the eastern city limits a historic heritage route in 1997, now a Pure Michigan Historic Byway.

The avenue had been platted in 1837, but its residential development came in the 1870s and 1880s. Bay City’s growth created a housing shortage, and wealthy lumber and salt families chose this neighborhood near the commercial district. When lumbering declined after the turn of the century, agriculture, iron and textiles took its place. Newly wealthy businessmen built among the earlier houses and farther east; development continued until the Great Depression. Preservation became a neighborhood effort in 2005, when residents began meeting and formed the Center Avenue Neighborhood Association. The association later helped the city administer a National Scenic Byways grant.

Follow Center Avenue east from Madison toward the city limits, moving through a district whose earliest construction lies in the west. The houses change from the Italianate James Shearer residence at 701 to the Queen Anne Frederick Bradley residence at 1400 and the steep-roofed Henry Clements residence at 1601. M-15 reaches the avenue on Trumbull Street and ends at the intersection.

moments.title: James Shearer Residence, 701 Center Avenue
moments.text: The James Shearer residence at 701 Center Avenue dates to 1876 and uses the Italianate style. The neighborhood developed in the 1870s and 1880s, attracting wealthy families from the lumber and salt trades to an address near Bay City’s commercial district. The earliest construction is concentrated in the district’s western part. The neighborhood has retained the residences and streetscapes that first made it a fashionable address.

moments.title: Frederick Bradley Residence, 1400 Center Avenue
moments.text: Two elaborate porches distinguish the Frederick Bradley residence at 1400 Center Avenue. Built from 1887 to 1889, the large Queen Anne house has an asymmetrical arrangement of rooms and building volumes. Its construction fell within the neighborhood’s nineteenth-century building period, before later houses introduced Prairie, Arts and Crafts and other twentieth-century styles.
moments.notice: Look for the Bradley house’s two elaborate porches and asymmetrical form.

moments.title: Henry Clements Residence, 1601 Center Avenue
moments.text: A steeply hipped roof marks the Henry Clements residence at 1601 Center Avenue. Built in 1890, the house uses a vernacular version of the Châteauesque style. That style joins Italianate, Stick, Queen Anne and Richardsonian Romanesque buildings in the residential district. The district’s original Center Avenue section and portions of Fifth and Sixth Avenues entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1982; its boundaries expanded in 2012.
moments.notice: The Clements house has a steeply hipped roof.
